diagnostic.question: Can you explain the main purpose of references, mutation, and shallow copy before reading?
diagnostic.answer: A complete answer should name the problem it solves, the values or control flow involved, and one mistake to avoid.

sections.title: Objects are reference values
sections.body: Two separate objects with the same properties are not strictly equal because they have different identities. Assigning an object to another variable copies the reference, so both bindings reach the same object. Primitive assignment copies the primitive value.

sections.title: Mutation is visible through every alias
sections.body: Changing sharedObject.name mutates the object, and every variable that references it observes the change. This can make data flow surprising when a function silently edits an argument. Prefer functions that return new values unless mutation is local, intentional, and documented.

sections.title: Spread copies one level
sections.body: {...original} and [...original] create a new outer container. Primitive fields are copied as values, but nested objects and arrays remain shared references. To update one nested path immutably, copy every container along that path.

sections.title: React relies on replacement
sections.body: React state should be treated as read-only. Mutating an existing object and passing the same reference can prevent a useful change signal and also changes old snapshots. Create the changed object or array and preserve untouched references where appropriate.

sections.title: Why this matters in React
sections.body: References, mutation, and shallow copy is part of the JavaScript model React code already uses. Components, event handlers, state updates, list rendering, and data requests become easier to reason about when this concept is understood without framework shortcuts. Practise the JavaScript behavior first, then identify the same rule in JSX or a component.

interviewQuestions.question: Explain references, mutation, and shallow copy to a junior developer.
interviewQuestions.answer: Compare primitive values and object identities. Recognize mutation through aliases. Know what a shallow copy does. Connect identity to React updates.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Show a small example and one common mistake.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you prove that code using references, mutation, and shallow copy behaves correctly?
interviewQuestions.answer: State the expected value or control flow first, test normal and boundary cases, and inspect the actual runtime result. Explain the JavaScript rule behind the evidence.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Which edge case would you test first?

interviewQuestions.question: Where can references, mutation, and shallow copy affect React code?
interviewQuestions.answer: It can affect values, callbacks, rendering decisions, updates, or data flow. The exact connection depends on the concept; the important step is to reason from JavaScript behavior before blaming React.

commonMistakes.symptom: Code using references, mutation, and shallow copy produces a surprising value.
commonMistakes.cause: The result was run before the value, type, scope, identity, or control flow was predicted.
commonMistakes.fix: Reduce the case, write the expected result, and apply the exact rule from the matching section.

commonMistakes.symptom: A learner copies syntax but cannot adapt it.
commonMistakes.cause: The example was memorized without explaining why it works.
commonMistakes.fix: Change the data and names, predict again, and explain which behavior must stay the same.

commonMistakes.symptom: A React problem is blamed on React immediately.
commonMistakes.cause: The underlying JavaScript behavior was not isolated first.
commonMistakes.fix: Reproduce the value or function behavior in a small JavaScript example, then reconnect it to the component.
